newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China gold mine jv sees licence this month.
newsitem.headline: China gold mine jv sees licence this month.

text.p: China's first gold mining joint venture, between Asia Minerals Corp. and the Zhaoyuan Gold Industrial Group (ZGIG), expects a business licence this month said Asia Minerals Corp. president David Owens on Monday.

"The approval process to obtain this business licence is bureaucratic, complex and extended," Owen said in a speech at the Asia Gold Congress being held in Hong Kong, noting that his firm had been negotiating with China since 1993.
Without a sufficient legal framework governing foreign investment in gold mining, Asia Minerals simply put its faith in State Planning Commission (SPC) approvals, Owen told Reuters.
"We decided that the SPC would provide for transferability of mining rights at an even more senior level," he said.
Foreign investors have been eyeing China's gold reserves ever since the country apparently threw open its doors to gold miners in 1993.

But effective foreign investment in China's gold mines was blocked by a clause preventing the transfer of exploration and mining rights -- essential to set up a working joint venture with a Chinese partner.

A gold-mining joint venture is legally established when China's State Administration for Industry and Commerce issues the company a business licence, Owen said, noting that to date no foreign mining company had obtained full state-level approval to mine gold in China.
The Yingezhuang joint venture is located in China's northeastern province of Shandong, which hold about a third of China's gold reserves, Owen said.
"Of that, our partners control about nine million ounces of reserves," Owen said.
Asia Minerals expects to invest a total of US$31.7 million in cash and equipment and expand the mine to produce 2,500 tonnes of ore per day from its current capacity of 450 tonnes.
"We hope the expansion will be complete by mid-1999," Owen said.
